claim: Parallel processing has been extensively studied in the low-level geniculostriate pathway and the high-level dorsal and ventral visual streams.
source: Although parallel processing has been extensively studied in the low-level geniculostriate pathway and the high-level dorsal and ventral visual streams, less is known at the intermediate-level visual areas.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of research in the field, supported by the broader scientific literature on visual processing.

claim: Less is known about parallel processing at the intermediate-level visual areas.
source: Although parallel processing has been extensively studied in the low-level geniculostriate pathway and the high-level dorsal and ventral visual streams, less is known at the intermediate-level visual areas.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field and motivates the study.

claim: This study employed high-resolution fMRI at 7T to investigate columnar and laminar organizations for color, disparity, and naturalistic texture in human V2.
source: In this study, we employed high-resolution fMRI at 7T to investigate the columnar and laminar organizations for color, disparity, and naturalistic texture in the human secondary visual cortex (V2), and their informational connectivity with lower- and higher-order visual areas.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: fMRI activations in V2 showed reproducible interdigitated color-selective thin and disparity-selective thick 'stripe' columns.
source: Although fMRI activations in V2 showed reproducible interdigitated color-selective thin and disparity-selective thick 'stripe' columns, we found no clear evidence of columnar organization for naturalistic textures.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: There is no clear evidence of columnar organization for naturalistic textures in V2.
source: Although fMRI activations in V2 showed reproducible interdigitated color-selective thin and disparity-selective thick 'stripe' columns, we found no clear evidence of columnar organization for naturalistic textures.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data and statistical analyses.

claim: Color-selectivity in V2 is strongest in the superficial layers.
source: Cortical depth-dependent analyses revealed the strongest color-selectivity in the superficial layers of V2, along with both feedforward and feedback informational connectivity with V1 and V4.
evidence: This is supported by cortical depth-dependent analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: V2 shows both feedforward and feedback informational connectivity with V1 and V4 for color processing.
source: Cortical depth-dependent analyses revealed the strongest color-selectivity in the superficial layers of V2, along with both feedforward and feedback informational connectivity with V1 and V4.
evidence: This is supported by informational connectivity analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Disparity selectivity was similar across different cortical depths of V2.
source: Disparity selectivity was similar across different cortical depths of V2, which showed significant feedforward and feedback connectivity with V1 and V3ab.
evidence: This is supported by cortical depth-dependent analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: V2 shows significant feedforward and feedback connectivity with V1 and V3ab for disparity processing.
source: Disparity selectivity was similar across different cortical depths of V2, which showed significant feedforward and feedback connectivity with V1 and V3ab.
evidence: This is supported by informational connectivity analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The selectivity for naturalistic texture was strongest in the deep layers of V2.
source: Interestingly, the selectivity for naturalistic texture was strongest in the deep layers of V2, with significant feedback connectivity from V4.
evidence: This is supported by cortical depth-dependent analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: V2 shows significant feedback connectivity from V4 for naturalistic texture processing.
source: Interestingly, the selectivity for naturalistic texture was strongest in the deep layers of V2, with significant feedback connectivity from V4.
evidence: This is supported by informational connectivity analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Local circuitry within cortical columns is crucial for processing color and disparity information in V2.
source: Thus, while local circuitry within cortical columns is crucial for processing color and disparity information, feedback signals from V4 are involved in generating the selectivity for naturalistic textures in area V2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on the observed columnar organization and laminar profiles.

claim: Feedback signals from V4 are involved in generating the selectivity for naturalistic textures in area V2.
source: Thus, while local circuitry within cortical columns is crucial for processing color and disparity information, feedback signals from V4 are involved in generating the selectivity for naturalistic textures in area V2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on the laminar profile and connectivity analysis.

claim: The retino-geniculate-striate pathway of the primate visual system is primarily segregated into magnocellular (M) and parvocellular (P) streams.
source: The retino-geniculate-striate pathway of the primate visual system is primarily segregated into magnocellular (M) and parvocellular (P) streams (Kaplan et al., 1990; Lee, 1996; Merigan and Maunsell, 1993), selectively processing different spatiotemporal frequencies of achromatic and chromatic information.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: M and P streams selectively process different spatiotemporal frequencies of achromatic and chromatic information.
source: The retino-geniculate-striate pathway of the primate visual system is primarily segregated into magnocellular (M) and parvocellular (P) streams (Kaplan et al., 1990; Lee, 1996; Merigan and Maunsell, 1993), selectively processing different spatiotemporal frequencies of achromatic and chromatic information.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In V1, M and P information from the geniculate are transformed into higher-level visual representations, such as motion, disparity, color, and orientation.
source: In the primary visual cortex (V1), M and P information from the geniculate are transformed into higher-level visual representations, such as motion, disparity, color, and orientation (Tootell and Nasr, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Early studies in nonhuman primates established the functional specializations of area V2.
source: Early studies in nonhuman primates established the functional specializations of area V2 (Burkhalter and Van Essen, 1986; Peterhans and von der Heydt, 1989; Poggio and Fischer, 1977; Zeki, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The processing of motion/disparity, color, and orientation information in V2 has been found to be organized into 'stripe'-shaped interdigitated columns.
source: The processing of motion/disparity, color, and orientation information has been found to be organized into 'stripe'-shaped interdigitated columns (DeYoe and Van Essen, 1985; Hubel and Livingstone, 1985; Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Roe and Ts'o, 1995; Ts'o et al., 2001; Xiao et al., 2003), corresponding to the 'thick', 'thin', and 'pale' stripes in cytochrome oxidase (CO) staining studies (Livingstone and Hubel, 1982; Tootell et al., 1983; referred to as CO-stripes in the present study).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The stripe-shaped columns in V2 correspond to the 'thick', 'thin', and 'pale' stripes in cytochrome oxidase (CO) staining studies.
source: The processing of motion/disparity, color, and orientation information has been found to be organized into 'stripe'-shaped interdigitated columns (DeYoe and Van Essen, 1985; Hubel and Livingstone, 1985; Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Roe and Ts'o, 1995; Ts'o et al., 2001; Xiao et al., 2003), corresponding to the 'thick', 'thin', and 'pale' stripes in cytochrome oxidase (CO) staining studies (Livingstone and Hubel, 1982; Tootell et al., 1983; referred to as CO-stripes in the present study).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Interdigitated columnar organizations for color and motion/disparity processing have been found in human V2 by high-resolution fMRI at 7T.
source: The interdigitated columnar organizations for color and motion/disparity processing have also been found in human V2 by high-resolution fMRI at 7T (Kennedy et al., 2023; Nasr et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Primate V2 was found to be sensitive to high-order statistical dependencies embedded in naturalistic textures.
source: More recently, primate V2 was also found to be sensitive to high-order statistical dependencies embedded in naturalistic textures (Freeman et al., 2013), a unique type of information critical for surface and material perception.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: High-order statistical dependencies in naturalistic textures are critical for surface and material perception.
source: More recently, primate V2 was also found to be sensitive to high-order statistical dependencies embedded in naturalistic textures (Freeman et al., 2013), a unique type of information critical for surface and material perception.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: High-order statistical dependencies in naturalistic textures are composed of correlations across different orientations, spatial scales, and local positions.
source: Computationally, these high-order statistical dependencies were composed of correlations across different orientations, spatial scales, and local positions, which can be calculated from the output of orientation filters in V1 (Freeman et al., 2013; Portilla and Simoncelli, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: High-order statistical dependencies can be calculated from the output of orientation filters in V1.
source: Computationally, these high-order statistical dependencies were composed of correlations across different orientations, spatial scales, and local positions, which can be calculated from the output of orientation filters in V1 (Freeman et al., 2013; Portilla and Simoncelli, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Naturalistic statistics are weakly represented in V1.
source: Although weakly represented in V1 (Freeman et al., 2013; Okazawa et al., 2015; Ziemba et al., 2016), the neural selectivity to naturalistic statistics was found to be increasingly stronger in the downstream areas V3 (Kohler et al., 2016) and V4 (Arcizet et al., 2008; Okazawa et al., 2015; Okazawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neural selectivity to naturalistic statistics is increasingly stronger in downstream areas V3 and V4.
source: Although weakly represented in V1 (Freeman et al., 2013; Okazawa et al., 2015; Ziemba et al., 2016), the neural selectivity to naturalistic statistics was found to be increasingly stronger in the downstream areas V3 (Kohler et al., 2016) and V4 (Arcizet et al., 2008; Okazawa et al., 2015; Okazawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings identified later and much weaker sensitivity to naturalistic texture in the superficial and deep layers of V1 compared to V2.
source: Electrophysiological recordings have also identified later and much weaker sensitivity to naturalistic texture in the superficial and deep layers of V1 compared to V2 (Ziemba et al., 2019), consistent with an effect of corticocortical feedback modulation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The weaker sensitivity to naturalistic texture in V1 compared to V2 is consistent with an effect of corticocortical feedback modulation.
source: Electrophysiological recordings have also identified later and much weaker sensitivity to naturalistic texture in the superficial and deep layers of V1 compared to V2 (Ziemba et al., 2019), consistent with an effect of corticocortical feedback modulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited research.

claim: It remains unclear whether the neural representations of naturalistic textures arise from local processing within V2 or feedback modulation from higher-order visual areas.
source: However, it remains unclear whether the neural representations of naturalistic textures arise from local processing within V2 or feedback modulation from higher-order visual areas, such as V4.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: If local circuits in area V2 are essential for processing high-order naturalistic statistics, specialized cortical columns might develop to enhance computational efficiency.
source: If local circuits in area V2 are essential for processing high-order naturalistic statistics, specialized cortical columns might develop to enhance computational efficiency (Mountcastle, 1997; Schulte To Brinke et al., 2022; Stoop et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on cited research about cortical organization.

claim: Pale stripes are known for their preferential responses to orientation information.
source: A likely candidate for such computational units is the pale stripes, known for their preferential responses to orientation information (Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Livingstone and Hubel, 1988; Lu and Roe, 2008; Malach et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: If feedback modulations from higher-order visual areas play a prominent role in generating selectivity to high-order statistical dependencies in V2, a specialized cortical column may not be necessary.
source: Alternatively, if feedback modulations from higher-order visual areas play a prominent role in generating the selectivity in area V2 to high-order statistical dependencies embedded in naturalist textures, a specialized cortical column may not be necessary for such computations.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the relationship between feedback processing and columnar organization.

claim: The integration of local elements across various locations, orientations, and spatial scales might pose a challenge for early visual areas like V2 to develop a specialized computational module.
source: Furthermore, the integration of local elements across various locations, orientations, and spatial scales, which is necessary for processing high-order statistics, might pose a challenge for early visual areas like V2 to develop a specialized computational module.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the computational challenges faced by V2.

claim: Cortical depth-dependent fMRI allows noninvasive measurement of feedforward, local, and feedback activity in human cerebral cortex.
source: Cortical depth-dependent fMRI (also called laminar fMRI) allows us to noninvasively measure feedforward, local, and feedback activity in human cerebral cortex (Huber et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2021; Norris and Polimeni, 2019; Olman et al., 2012; Polimeni and Uludağ, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Color-selective activation was defined as the contrast of fMRI responses between chromatic and achromatic gratings.
source: Color-selective activation was defined as the contrast of fMRI responses between chromatic (Chr) and achromatic (Ach) gratings (first column).
evidence: This describes the operational definition used in the study.

claim: Disparity-selective activation was the response difference between disparity-defined sinusoidal gratings by random dot stereograms and their zero-disparity counterparts.
source: Disparity-selective activation was the response difference between disparity-defined sinusoidal gratings (3D) by random dot stereograms (RDSs) and their zero-disparity (2D) counterparts (second column).
evidence: This describes the operational definition used in the study.

claim: Texture-selective activation was the response difference between naturalistic textures and spectrally matched noise.
source: Texture-selective activation was the response difference between naturalistic textures (T) and spectrally matched noise (N) (third column).
evidence: This describes the operational definition used in the study.

claim: Neural selectivity to binocular disparity has been found in layer 4B of V1, V2 thick stripes, and V3ab in the dorsal stream.
source: Previous studies in anesthetized macaques found neural selectivity to binocular disparity in the layer 4B of V1, V2 thick stripes, and V3ab in the dorsal stream (Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Livingstone and Hubel, 1987; Tootell et al., 1983; Ts'o et al., 2001; Tsao et al., 2003), color selectivity in the color blobs in the V1 superficial layers, V2 thin stripes, and V4 in the ventral stream (Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Livingstone and Hubel, 1987; Livingstone and Hubel, 1988; Lu and Roe, 2008; Zeki, 1973), and strong orientation selectivity in layer 2/3 of V1, V2 pale stripes, and V4 (Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Roe and Ts'o, 1995; Tanigawa et al., 2010; Ts'o et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Color selectivity has been found in the color blobs in the V1 superficial layers, V2 thin stripes, and V4 in the ventral stream.
source: Previous studies in anesthetized macaques found neural selectivity to binocular disparity in the layer 4B of V1, V2 thick stripes, and V3ab in the dorsal stream (Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Livingstone and Hubel, 1987; Tootell et al., 1983; Ts'o et al., 2001; Tsao et al., 2003), color selectivity in the color blobs in the V1 superficial layers, V2 thin stripes, and V4 in the ventral stream (Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Livingstone and Hubel, 1987; Livingstone and Hubel, 1988; Lu and Roe, 2008; Zeki, 1973), and strong orientation selectivity in layer 2/3 of V1, V2 pale stripes, and V4 (Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Roe and Ts'o, 1995; Tanigawa et al., 2010; Ts'o et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Strong orientation selectivity has been found in layer 2/3 of V1, V2 pale stripes, and V4.
source: Previous studies in anesthetized macaques found neural selectivity to binocular disparity in the layer 4B of V1, V2 thick stripes, and V3ab in the dorsal stream (Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Livingstone and Hubel, 1987; Tootell et al., 1983; Ts'o et al., 2001; Tsao et al., 2003), color selectivity in the color blobs in the V1 superficial layers, V2 thin stripes, and V4 in the ventral stream (Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Livingstone and Hubel, 1987; Livingstone and Hubel, 1988; Lu and Roe, 2008; Zeki, 1973), and strong orientation selectivity in layer 2/3 of V1, V2 pale stripes, and V4 (Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Roe and Ts'o, 1995; Tanigawa et al., 2010; Ts'o et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There are connections between V1 interblobs and thick stripes.
source: There are also other connections, such as V1 interblobs projecting to thick stripes (Federer et al., 2021; Hu and Roe, 2022; Sincich and Horton, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Naturalistic textures might be selectively processed by orientation-selective neurons in the pale stripes of V2.
source: Given a strong dependency on the output of orientation filters (Portilla and Simoncelli, 2000; Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001), naturalistic textures might be selectively processed by orientation-selective neurons in the pale stripes of V2.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on cited research about texture processing.

claim: Feedback modulations may play important roles in processing visual information, especially in conscious visual perception.
source: In addition to feedforward and local horizontal connections, feedback modulations may also play important roles in processing visual information, especially in conscious visual perception (Ge et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: There are feedforward connections from V1 to V4.
source: There are also other connections such as feedforward connections from V1 to V4 (Ungerleider et al., 2008), and feedback connections from the superficial layers to lower-order visual areas (Briggs, 2020; Rockland and Pandya, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: There are feedback connections from the superficial layers to lower-order visual areas.
source: There are also other connections such as feedforward connections from V1 to V4 (Ungerleider et al., 2008), and feedback connections from the superficial layers to lower-order visual areas (Briggs, 2020; Rockland and Pandya, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Color-selective and disparity-selective stripe-shaped activations in V2 are arranged perpendicular to the V1-V2 border.
source: Color-selective and disparity-selective stripe-shaped activations arranged perpendicular to the V1-V2 border.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and described in the text.

claim: Texture-selective activations are found in anterior V2 corresponding to peripheral visual field.
source: Black arrowheads in the fourth column highlight the texture-selective activations in anterior V2 (corresponding to peripheral visual field).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and described in the text.

claim: The inter-session correlation coefficient for color-selective activation maps in subject S09 is r = 0.66 (p<0.001, FWE corrected).
source: For the representative subject (Figure 2B), the correlation coefficients for both color- (r = 0.66) and disparity-selective activation maps (r = 0.53) were highly significant (both p<0.001, family-wise-error [FWE] corrected; activation patterns from the two sessions were shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The inter-session correlation coefficient for disparity-selective activation maps in subject S09 is r = 0.53 (p<0.001, FWE corrected).
source: For the representative subject (Figure 2B), the correlation coefficients for both color- (r = 0.66) and disparity-selective activation maps (r = 0.53) were highly significant (both p<0.001, family-wise-error [FWE] corrected; activation patterns from the two sessions were shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The interdigitated columnar organizations for color and disparity processing are highly reproducible.
source: These findings demonstrate that the interdigitated columnar organizations for color and disparity processing are highly reproducible.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the inter-session correlation analysis.

claim: Thin- and thick-stripe ROIs show the strongest selectivity to color and disparity information, respectively.
source: From the columnar response profile (Figure 2D), thin- and thick-stripe ROIs show the strongest selectivity to color and disparity information, respectively.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and described in the text.

claim: There is no significant difference in texture-selectivity index across three different stripes (F(2,9) = 1.88, p=0.18, BF10 = 0.65).
source: We further conducted repeated-measures ANOVA and Bayesian ANOVA to examine whether there is difference in texture-selectivity index across three different stripes. The results were statistically nonsignificant (F(2,9) = 1.88, p=0.18, BF10 = 0.65).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Texture selectivity increased significantly with eccentricity (F(2,9) = 17.74, p<0.001, BF10 = 345.83).
source: Texture selectivity increased significantly with eccentricity (Figure 2D, F(2,9) = 17.74, p<0.001, BF10 = 345.83; peripheral vs. parafoveal: t(9) = 4.12, p<0.01; parafoveal vs. central: t(9) = 3.20, p<0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Texture selectivity in V2 is stronger in more peripheral visual fields.
source: These findings suggest that texture selectivity in V2 is stronger in more peripheral visual fields.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the eccentricity analysis.

claim: The central visual field might prefer texture patterns with a higher spatial frequency than the stimuli used in this study.
source: However, it is possible that the central visual field might prefer texture patterns with a higher spatial frequency than our stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculation about the results.

claim: All texture families showed significantly stronger activation in V2 compared to the corresponding noise patterns in the 3T experiment.
source: All texture families showed significantly stronger activation in V2 compared to the corresponding noise patterns, even for those that 'appeared' to have residual texture information (e.g., the third texture family).
evidence: This is a result from the 3T validation experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: The 3T data showed a notable increase in texture-selective activations compared to the 7T experiment, likely due to the increased stimulus presentation speed.
source: The 3T data also showed a notable increase in texture-selective activations compared to the 7T experiment, likely due to the increased stimulus presentation speed.
evidence: This is an observation and interpretation from the 3T validation experiment.

claim: Color selectivity was significantly stronger in the superficial cortical depth compared to the middle and deep cortical depths in V1 (F(2,9) = 15.08, p<0.001, BF10 = 133.72).
source: Color selectivity was significantly stronger in the superficial cortical depth compared to the middle and deep cortical depths in both V1 (F(2,9) = 15.08, p<0.001, BF10 = 133.72; S vs. M: t(9) = 4.70, p<0.01; S vs. D: t(9) = 4.12, p<0.01) and V2 (F(2,9) = 12.93, p<0.001, BF10 = 64.83; S vs. M: t(9) = 3.77, p<0.01; S vs. D: t(9) = 3.85, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cortical depth-dependent analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Color selectivity was significantly stronger in the superficial cortical depth compared to the middle and deep cortical depths in V2 (F(2,9) = 12.93, p<0.001, BF10 = 64.83).
source: Color selectivity was significantly stronger in the superficial cortical depth compared to the middle and deep cortical depths in both V1 (F(2,9) = 15.08, p<0.001, BF10 = 133.72; S vs. M: t(9) = 4.70, p<0.01; S vs. D: t(9) = 4.12, p<0.01) and V2 (F(2,9) = 12.93, p<0.001, BF10 = 64.83; S vs. M: t(9) = 3.77, p<0.01; S vs. D: t(9) = 3.85, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cortical depth-dependent analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The strongest color selectivity in the superficial cortical depth is consistent with the fact that color blobs locate in the superficial layers of V1.
source: According to the hierarchical model, the strongest color selectivity in the superficial cortical depth is consistent with the fact that color blobs locate in the superficial layers of V1 (Figure 1B, Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Nassi and Callaway, 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited research and the hierarchical model.

claim: The strongest color selectivity in superficial V2 suggests that both local and feedforward connections are involved in processing color information.
source: The strongest color selectivity in superficial V2 suggests that both local and feedforward connections are involved in processing color information (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the laminar profile results.

claim: Disparity selectivity was significantly higher in the superficial cortical depth compared to the middle and deep cortical depths in V3ab (F(2,9) = 9.06, p<0.01, BF10 = 16.81).
source: Disparity selectivity was significantly higher in the superficial cortical depth compared to the middle and deep cortical depths in V3ab (Figure 3B) (F(2,9) = 9.06, p<0.01, BF10 = 16.81; S vs. M: t(9) = 3.11, p<0.05; S vs. D: t(9) = 3.75, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cortical depth-dependent analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The absence of laminar difference in disparity selectivity in V2 may suggest that both feedforward, feedback, and local mechanisms are involved in processing disparity information.
source: The absence of laminar difference in disparity selectivity may suggest that both feedforward, feedback, and local mechanisms are involved in processing disparity information in area V2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the laminar profile results.

claim: Response selectivity to naturalistic texture was strongest in the deep cortical depth in V1 (F(2,9) = 12.91, p<0.001, BF10 = 63.57).
source: Response selectivity to naturalistic texture was strongest in the deep cortical depth in both V1 (F(2,9) = 12.91, p<0.001, BF10 = 63.57; D vs. M: t(9) = 2.28, p<0.05; D vs. S: t(9) = 4.76, p<0.01) and V2 (F(2,9) = 8.6, BF10 = 14.08, p<0.01; D vs. M: t(9) = 2.49, p<0.05; D vs. S: t(9) = 4.29, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cortical depth-dependent analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Response selectivity to naturalistic texture was strongest in the deep cortical depth in V2 (F(2,9) = 8.6, BF10 = 14.08, p<0.01).
source: Response selectivity to naturalistic texture was strongest in the deep cortical depth in both V1 (F(2,9) = 12.91, p<0.001, BF10 = 63.57; D vs. M: t(9) = 2.28, p<0.05; D vs. S: t(9) = 4.76, p<0.01) and V2 (F(2,9) = 8.6, BF10 = 14.08, p<0.01; D vs. M: t(9) = 2.49, p<0.05; D vs. S: t(9) = 4.29, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cortical depth-dependent analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Texture selectivity in V4 and V3ab showed no significant difference across cortical depths.
source: Texture selectivity showed no significant difference across cortical depths in the higher-level visual areas V4 (F(2,9) = 1.64, p=0.22) or V3ab (F(2,9) = 3.53, p=0.051), which were significantly larger than those in V1 and V2 (all paired comparisons between ROIs, p<0.001, BF10 > 1106.79).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cortical depth-dependent analysis.

claim: Texture selectivity in V4 and V3ab was significantly larger than in V1 and V2.
source: Texture selectivity showed no significant difference across cortical depths in the higher-level visual areas V4 (F(2,9) = 1.64, p=0.22) or V3ab (F(2,9) = 3.53, p=0.051), which were significantly larger than those in V1 and V2 (all paired comparisons between ROIs, p<0.001, BF10 > 1106.79).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cortical depth-dependent analysis.

claim: V1 responses to naturalistic textures were significantly weaker compared to spectrally matched noise.
source: V1 responses to naturalistic textures were also significantly weaker compared to spectrally matched noise, in line with the top-down feedback hypothesis of predictive coding (Friston, 2005; Murray et al., 2002; Rao and Ballard, 1999).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis, interpreted in the context of predictive coding.

claim: The strongest selectivity in the deep layers of V2 suggests that feedback modulations from higher-level visual areas play a crucial role in processing naturalistic statistical information in this region.
source: The strongest selectivity in the deep layers of V2 suggests that feedback modulations from higher-level visual areas play a crucial role in processing naturalistic statistical information in this region.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the laminar profile results.

claim: For color-selective processing, significant feedforward (t(9) = 5.64, p<0.001) and feedback connections (t(9) = 10.39, p<0.001) were found between V1 and V2.
source: As shown in Figure 4, for color-selective processing, significant feedforward (t(9) = 5.64, p<0.001) and feedback connections (t(9) = 10.39, p<0.001) were found between V1 and V2, and between V2 and V4 (both t(9) > 4.96, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the informational connectivity analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: For color-selective processing, significant feedforward and feedback connections were found between V2 and V4 (both t(9) > 4.96, p<0.01).
source: As shown in Figure 4, for color-selective processing, significant feedforward (t(9) = 5.64, p<0.001) and feedback connections (t(9) = 10.39, p<0.001) were found between V1 and V2, and between V2 and V4 (both t(9) > 4.96, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the informational connectivity analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: For disparity-selective processing, significant feedforward (t(9) = 3.77, p<0.05) and feedback connections (t(9) = 3.06, p<0.05) were found between V1 and V2.
source: For disparity-selective processing, significant feedforward (t(9) = 3.77, p<0.05) and feedback connections (t(9) = 3.06, p<0.05) were found between V1 and V2, and also between V2 and V3ab (both t(9) > 2.90, p<0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the informational connectivity analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: For disparity-selective processing, significant feedforward and feedback connections were found between V2 and V3ab (both t(9) > 2.90, p<0.05).
source: For disparity-selective processing, significant feedforward (t(9) = 3.77, p<0.05) and feedback connections (t(9) = 3.06, p<0.05) were found between V1 and V2, and also between V2 and V3ab (both t(9) > 2.90, p<0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the informational connectivity analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: For naturalistic texture-selective processing, a significant feedback connection was found from V4 to V2 (t(9) = 4.28, p<0.05).
source: In contrast, for naturalistic texture-selective processing, a significant feedback connection was found from V4 to V2 (t(9) = 4.28, p<0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the informational connectivity analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Color- and disparity-selective activations revealed clear stripe-shaped columnar organizations in area V2, oriented perpendicular to the V1-V2 border.
source: Color- and disparity-selective activations revealed clear stripe-shaped columnar organizations in area V2, oriented perpendicular to the V1-V2 border (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The columnar patterns for color and disparity were reproducible between different scanning sessions.
source: These columnar patterns were reproducible between different scanning sessions (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and are consistent with previous findings from intrinsic optical imaging studies in monkeys (Lu and Roe, 2008; Ts'o et al., 2001) and 7T fMRI studies in humans (Kennedy et al., 2023; Nasr et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the inter-session correlation analysis and cited research.

claim: The columnar patterns for color and disparity are consistent with previous findings from intrinsic optical imaging studies in monkeys and 7T fMRI studies in humans.
source: These columnar patterns were reproducible between different scanning sessions (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and are consistent with previous findings from intrinsic optical imaging studies in monkeys (Lu and Roe, 2008; Ts'o et al., 2001) and 7T fMRI studies in humans (Kennedy et al., 2023; Nasr et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CO-stripes in V2 exhibit similar texture selectivity.
source: However, we found no clear evidence for modular organization for naturalistic textures. CO-stripes in V2 exhibit similar texture selectivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the ROI analysis.

claim: Cortical depth-dependent analysis revealed that compared to color and disparity information, the processing of naturalistic statistics in V2 is more dependent on feedback modulation from V4.
source: Cortical depth-dependent analysis revealed that compared to color and disparity information, the processing of naturalistic statistics in V2 is more dependent on feedback modulation from V4.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the laminar profile and connectivity analyses.

claim: The laminar profiles of response selectivity revealed both inter- and intra-areal hierarchical processing of visual information.
source: The laminar profiles of response selectivity revealed both inter- and intra-areal hierarchical processing of visual information.
evidence: This is a general conclusion from the laminar analysis.

claim: Color blobs are primarily located in the superficial layers of primate V1.
source: This result is consistent with the findings that color blobs are primarily located in the superficial layers of primate V1 (Livingstone and Hubel, 1982), and that the local processing of color information is most prominent in the superficial layers of the early visual cortex (Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Lu and Roe, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The local processing of color information is most prominent in the superficial layers of the early visual cortex.
source: This result is consistent with the findings that color blobs are primarily located in the superficial layers of primate V1 (Livingstone and Hubel, 1982), and that the local processing of color information is most prominent in the superficial layers of the early visual cortex (Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Lu and Roe, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The middle layer is recognized as the primary termination of feedforward inputs.
source: This result suggests that feedforward, feedback, and local mechanisms all contribute to generating disparity-defined 3D perception as the middle layer is recognized as the primary termination of feedforward inputs, and the superficial and deep layers are considered as the output layers to higher-order areas and the primary recipients of feedback projections, respectively (Callaway, 2004; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on cortical circuitry.

claim: The superficial and deep layers are considered as the output layers to higher-order areas and the primary recipients of feedback projections, respectively.
source: This result suggests that feedforward, feedback, and local mechanisms all contribute to generating disparity-defined 3D perception as the middle layer is recognized as the primary termination of feedforward inputs, and the superficial and deep layers are considered as the output layers to higher-order areas and the primary recipients of feedback projections, respectively (Callaway, 2004; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on cortical circuitry.

claim: Both feedforward and feedback signals play important roles in color and disparity processing in the ventral (V2-V4) and dorsal (V2-V3ab) visual streams.
source: Consistent with the laminar response profiles, cortical depth-dependent informational connectivity analyses showed that both feedforward and feedback signals play important roles in color and disparity processing in the ventral (i.e., V2-V4) and dorsal (i.e., V2-V3ab) visual streams, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the connectivity analysis.

claim: A previous electrophysiological study found that the superficial and deep layers of V1 are subject to top-down modulation from higher-order visual areas during processing of naturalistic textures.
source: A previous electrophysiological study investigated laminar neural activity in V1 and V2 to naturalistic textures in anesthetized macaques (Ziemba et al., 2019). Their findings suggest that the superficial and deep layers of V1 are subject to top-down modulation from higher-order visual areas during processing of naturalistic textures.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The strongest signal reduction in the superficial cortical depth is consistent with the model of canonical microcircuits for predictive coding.
source: This could also explain the strongest signal reduction in the superficial cortical depth in our results since the error signals should be mainly represented in the output layers according to the model of canonical microcircuits for predictive coding (Bastos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited research on predictive coding.

claim: Ziemba et al., 2019 found stronger texture selectivity in the superficial and middle layers of V2.
source: In V2, Ziemba et al., 2019 found stronger texture selectivity in the superficial and middle layers, which potentially emerged from local processing within this area.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The amount of texture selectivity in V4 was stronger compared to V2.
source: The amount of texture selectivity in V4 was also stronger compared to V2. This is consistent with previous macaque studies showing stronger texture selectivity in V4 than in V2 (Okazawa et al., 2017) and local clustered neurons in V4 that shared preferred image statistics (Hatanaka et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis, consistent with cited research.

claim: Previous macaque studies showed stronger texture selectivity in V4 than in V2.
source: The amount of texture selectivity in V4 was also stronger compared to V2. This is consistent with previous macaque studies showing stronger texture selectivity in V4 than in V2 (Okazawa et al., 2017) and local clustered neurons in V4 that shared preferred image statistics (Hatanaka et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Local clustered neurons in V4 share preferred image statistics.
source: The amount of texture selectivity in V4 was also stronger compared to V2. This is consistent with previous macaque studies showing stronger texture selectivity in V4 than in V2 (Okazawa et al., 2017) and local clustered neurons in V4 that shared preferred image statistics (Hatanaka et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Pilot analyses suggest modular organizations for naturalistic texture, in addition to those for color and disparity in V4 and V3ab.
source: In addition, our pilot analyses also suggest modular organizations for naturalistic texture, in addition to those for color and disparity in V4 and V3ab (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is a preliminary finding shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: General anesthesia may have substantially reduced feedback modulation from high-order brain areas in the monkey study.
source: In the monkey study, it is possible that general anesthesia substantially reduced feedback modulation from high-order brain areas.
evidence: This is a speculation about the differences between the current study and previous research.

claim: V4 activity is more closely related to conscious visual perception than the early visual areas.
source: There is evidence showing that V4 activity is more closely related to conscious visual perception than the early visual areas (Mehta et al., 2000; Tong, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Top-down feedback might reduce the neural activity representing prediction errors in the superficial layers of lower-order areas, counteracting the effect of neural response evoked by local processing.
source: In accordance with the predictive coding hypothesis discussed above, top-down feedback might reduce the neural activity representing prediction errors in the superficial layers of lower-order areas, counteracting the effect of neural response evoked by local processing.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the predictive coding framework.

claim: The cortical processing of naturalistic textures depends on the type of statistical regularities.
source: Furthermore, recent macaque studies have shown that the cortical processing of naturalistic textures depends on the type of statistical regularities (Kim et al., 2022; Okazawa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Texture selectivity across neurons in V2 and V4 can be highly diversified.
source: As suggested by the previous findings, texture selectivity across neurons in V2 and V4 can be highly diversified (Figure 2e in Freeman et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2022): some texture families are much more or less effective in driving neural activity than others, with distinct temporal dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A cortical column is formed by many mini-columns bound together by short-range horizontal connections.
source: A cortical column is formed by many mini-columns bound together by short-range horizontal connections (Mountcastle, 1997), supporting efficient information processing via local circuitry.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The absence of a columnar organization in area V2 for texture is consistent with a dominant role of feedback modulation, rather than local or feedforward processing.
source: Thus, the absence of a columnar organization in area V2 is consistent with a dominant role of feedback modulation, rather than local or feedforward processing in generating texture selectivity within this area.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: V4 neurons are more suitable for processing naturalistic textures than those in V2.
source: Considering the complex computations required for processing naturalistic information, it is likely that V4 neurons are more suitable for this task than those in V2.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the complexity of texture processing.

claim: The neural tunings in V4 are distributed in a way suitable for categorizing textures and predicting texture discrimination abilities.
source: In line with this idea, the neural tunings in V4 are distributed in a way suitable for categorizing textures and predicting texture discrimination abilities (Hatanaka et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2022; Okazawa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Texture-selective organizations in V4 and V3ab may be related to surface representations in these higher-order visual areas.
source: Consistently, our results also revealed modular organizations for textures in V4 and V3ab (Figure 2—figure supplement 8). These texture-selective organizations may be related to surface representations in these higher-order visual areas (Wang et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings and cited research.

claim: Cortical columns in V2 are much larger than those in V1.
source: Although cortical columns in V2 are much larger than those in V1 (Lu and Roe, 2007), our results do not rule out the possibility that smaller modules of texture processing might exist beyond our fMRI resolution at 1 mm isotropic voxels, especially at farther eccentricities (Figure 2A and D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The critical period for the formation of cortical columns in lower-level visual areas might close at an earlier stage during development.
source: Finally, the critical period for the formation of cortical columns in lower-level visual areas might close at an earlier stage during development (Kiorpes, 2015; Levi, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The emergence of selectivity to naturalistic textures may require extensive visual experience with the ability to actively explore the natural environment.
source: It is possible that the emergence of selectivity to naturalistic textures requires extensive visual experience with the ability to actively explore the natural environment.
evidence: This is a speculation about the development of texture selectivity.

claim: After the closure of the critical period in V2 for forming color- and disparity-selective columns, V4 may still be in its critical period with high neural plasticity.
source: After the closure of the critical period in V2 for forming color- and disparity-selective columns, V4 may still be in its critical period with high neural plasticity, allowing it to develop neuronal clusters with strong preference for naturalistic textures (Hatanaka et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculation about developmental timing, supported by a citation.

claim: Feedback modulations from V4 may further increase the selectivity for naturalistic textures in V2.
source: Subsequently, feedback modulations from V4 may further increase the selectivity for naturalistic textures in V2.
evidence: This is a speculation about the role of feedback in texture processing.

claim: Different cortical mechanisms may be involved at various processing stages for different types of naturalistic textures.
source: Given the diversity of naturalistic textures, different cortical mechanisms may be involved at various processing stages (Kim et al., 2022; Okazawa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The original BOLD responses were strongly biased toward the superficial depth due to the sensitivity of T2*w GE-BOLD signal to large draining veins.
source: Due to the limitations of the T2*w GE-BOLD signal in its sensitivity to large draining veins (Fracasso et al., 2021; Parkes et al., 2005; Uludag and Havlicek, 2021), the original BOLD responses were strongly biased toward the superficial depth in our data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a limitation of the method, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: VASO-CBV and SE-BOLD fMRI techniques have higher spatial specificity but much lower sensitivity compared to GE-BOLD.
source: Compared to GE-BOLD, VASO-CBV and SE-BOLD fMRI techniques have higher spatial specificity but much lower sensitivity (Huber et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Differential BOLD signals in a continuous stimulus design exhibit stronger microvascular contribution, which might help improve the laminar specificity of feature selectivity measures.
source: As suggested by previous studies (Kim and Fukuda, 2008; Qian et al., 2024; Yacoub et al., 2008), differential BOLD signals in a continuous stimulus design exhibit stronger microvascular contribution, which might help improve the laminar specificity of feature selectivity measures in our results (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: 7T fMRI at 1 mm isotropic resolution can resolve cortical depth-dependent signals in human visual cortex.
source: However, consistent with our results, previous studies have also shown that 7T fMRI at 1 mm isotropic resolution can resolve cortical depth-dependent signals in human visual cortex (Roefs et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The interpretations of cortical depth-dependent results are based on the canonical models of cortical microcircuitry.
source: Finally, the interpretations of cortical depth-dependent results are based on the canonical models of cortical microcircuitry.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical framework used for interpretation.

claim: Alternative connections exist in addition to the major pathways in the canonical models of cortical microcircuitry.
source: Alternative connections exist in addition to these major pathways.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging the complexity of cortical circuitry.

claim: The findings on cortical microcircuitry in humans would require further support from invasive neuroscience methods, such as laminar electrophysiological recordings in non-human primates.
source: Therefore, our findings on the cortical microcircuitry in humans would require further support from invasive neuroscience methods, such as laminar electrophysiological recordings in non-human primates.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study and the need for further validation.

claim: Ten participants (four females; age range 21–40 years) were recruited for this study.
source: Ten participants (four females; age range 21–40 years) were recruited for this study.
evidence: This describes the study participants.

claim: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and reported no history of neuropsychological or visual disorders.
source: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and reported no history of neuropsychological or visual disorders.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for participants.

claim: A sample size of 10 participants is relatively large according to the literature on columnar and laminar fMRI studies with long scanning durations.
source: A sample size of 10 participants is relatively large according to the literature on columnar and laminar fMRI studies with long scanning durations (Nasr et al., 2016; Tootell and Nasr, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The experimental procedures were approved by the ethical review board of Institute of Biophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (no. 2012-IRB-011).
source: The experimental procedures were approved by the ethical review board of Institute of Biophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (no. 2012-IRB-011).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to their participation in the study.
source: Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to their participation in the study.
evidence: This describes the ethical procedures for the study.

claim: Visual stimuli subtended 46.7° × 35.9° in visual angle.
source: Visual stimuli subtended 46.7° × 35.9° in visual angle, with a fixation point (0.3° in diameter) in the center.
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters.

claim: The isoluminance level varied significantly with eccentricity for blue-gray (F(2,9) = 87.9, p<0.001, FWE corrected) and blue-red (F(2,9) = 35.71, p<0.001, FWE corrected).
source: Consistent with previous findings (Nasr et al., 2016; Bilodeau and Faubert, 1997; Livingstone and Hubel, 1987; Mullen, 1985), the isoluminance level varied significantly as eccentricity (blue-gray: F(2,9) = 87.9, p<0.001, FWE corrected; blue-red: F(2,9) = 35.71, p<0.001, FWE corrected).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the isoluminance adjustment procedure, consistent with cited research.

claim: MRI data were acquired on a 7T MAGNETOM MRI scanner with a custom-built 32-channel receive and 4-channel transmit open-face surface coil.
source: MRI data were acquired on a 7T MAGNETOM MRI scanner (Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany) with a custom-built 32-channel receive and 4-channel transmit open-face surface coil (Sengupta et al., 2016), in the Beijing MRI center for Brain Research.
evidence: This describes the MRI acquisition setup.

claim: Functional data were collected with a T2*-weighted 2D GE-EPI sequence at 1.0 mm isotropic voxels.
source: Functional data were collected with a T2*-weighted 2D GE-EPI sequence (1.0 mm isotropic voxels, 39 slices, TR = 2400 ms, TE = 25 ms, image matrix = 128 × 128, FOV = 128 × 128 mm2, GRAPPA acceleration factor = 3, nominal flip angle = 80°, partial Fourier factor = 7/8, phase encoding direction from head to foot, receiver bandwidth = 1148 Hz/Pix).
evidence: This describes the fMRI acquisition parameters.

claim: High-resolution anatomical volumes were acquired with a T1-weighted MP2RAGE sequence at 0.7 mm isotropic resolution.
source: High-resolution anatomical volumes were acquired with a T1-weighted MP2RAGE sequence at 0.7 mm isotropic resolution (256 sagittal slices, centric phase encoding, acquisition matrix = 320 × 320, FOV = 224 × 224 mm2, GRAPPA = 3, TR = 4000 ms, TE = 3.05 ms, TI1=750 ms, flip angle = 4°, TI2 = 2500 ms, flip angle = 5°).
evidence: This describes the anatomical MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: A bite-bar was used to minimize head motion to ensure high data quality.
source: A bite-bar was settled for each subject to minimize head motion to ensure high data quality.
evidence: This describes a methodological detail to improve data quality.

claim: An equi-volume method was used to calculate the relative cortical depth of each voxel.
source: An equi-volume method was used to calculate the relative cortical depth of each voxel to the white matter and pial surface (0: white matter surface; 1: pial surface, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), using mripy (https://github.com/herrlich10/mripy).
evidence: This describes the method for cortical depth calculation.

claim: The voxels in each ROI were divided into three bins: deep depth (0–0.33), middle depth (0.33–0.67), and superficial depth (0.67–1.00).
source: The voxels in each ROI were sorted and divided into three bins: deep depth (0–0.33), middle depth (0.33–0.67), and superficial depth (0.67–1.00) (Ge et al., 2020; Kemper et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the method for defining cortical depth bins, supported by citations.

claim: Surface ROIs for V1, V2, V3ab, and V4 were defined based on the polar angle atlas from the 7T retinotopic dataset of Human Connectome Project.
source: Surface ROIs for V1, V2, V3ab, and V4 were defined based on the polar angle atlas from the 7T retinotopic dataset of Human Connectome Project (Benson et al., 2014; Benson et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the method for ROI definition, supported by citations.

claim: The top 5% cortical vertices with large signal changes from baseline and the corresponding voxels across all cortical depths were excluded from analysis to mitigate the strong BOLD effect from large pial veins.
source: To mitigate the strong BOLD effect from large pial veins on layer-specific signals in the gray matter (Cheng et al., 2001; Gati et al., 1997; Kay et al., 2019; Yacoub et al., 2005), we excluded vertices with extremely large signal changes and their corresponding voxels in the gray matter. Specifically, the top 5% cortical vertices with large signal changes from baseline (all stimulus conditions vs. fixation) and the corresponding voxels across all cortical depths were excluded from analysis in V1, V2, V4, and V3ab (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This describes a methodological approach to reduce vascular artifacts, supported by citations.

claim: This large vein removal approach can effectively reduce the superficial bias in laminar response profiles of the visual cortex.
source: According to our previous study (Liu et al., 2021), this large vein removal approach can effectively reduce the superficial bias in laminar response profiles of the visual cortex.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Feedforward connectivity was defined as the connection between the superficial layer of the lower visual area and the middle layer of the higher visual area.
source: Specifically, feedforward connectivity was defined as the connection between the superficial layer of the lower visual area and the middle layer of the higher visual area, whereas feedback connectivity was defined as the connection between two deep layers (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the operational definition used in the connectivity analysis.

claim: Feedback connectivity was defined as the connection between two deep layers.
source: Specifically, feedforward connectivity was defined as the connection between the superficial layer of the lower visual area and the middle layer of the higher visual area, whereas feedback connectivity was defined as the connection between two deep layers (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the operational definition used in the connectivity analysis.
